title: Olives: fat, fiber, salt and calories

seo.title: Olives: fat, fiber, sodium and calories
seo.meta_description: Olives are rich in monounsaturated fat and can be very high in sodium from curing. See numbers per 100 g and a realistic 30 g serving.
seo.search_intent: Understand calories, fat, fiber and sodium in olives and what a serving provides

excerpt: Olives are a fatty fruit rather than a sugary one. A current USDA green-olive reference provides about 145 calories, 15.3 g fat, 3.3 g fiber and 1,556 mg sodium per 100 g. In a 30 g serving, that is about 44 calories, 4.6 g fat, 1.0 g fiber and roughly 467 mg sodium. Sodium is the number most likely to vary substantially among brands and curing styles.
content_html:
Olives behave differently from most fresh fruit: much of their energy comes from fat rather than sugar. And because table olives are almost always cured, sodium can matter as much as calories.

What a green-olive reference provides

The USDA reference used here contains per 100 g about 145 calories, 15.3 g fat, 3.3 g fiber, 3.8 g carbohydrate and 1,556 mg sodium. About 11.3 g of the fat is monounsaturated.

A 30 g serving comes to roughly 44 calories, 4.6 g fat, 1.0 g fiber and 467 mg sodium.

Are olives high in calories?

They are more energy-dense than many fresh fruits because they contain oil, but a typical serving is small. A per-100-g comparison can make olives look much more caloric than the handful that actually appears on a snack plate.

Energy also varies among products. A legacy USDA reference for canned ripe olives provides about 116 calories/100 g versus 145 in the green example.

Most of the fat is monounsaturated

Oleic acid makes up a large share of olive fat. It is the same characteristic monounsaturated fatty acid found in olive oil, while the whole olive also retains water, fiber, skin and other fruit components.

Sodium is the label number worth watching

The 1,556 mg sodium/100 g in the green reference is high, but it does not describe every olive. Brine strength, curing method, rinsing and brand formulation can move the number dramatically.

The ripe canned reference used for context contains about 735 mg sodium/100 g, less than half as much. That does not mean black olives are automatically lower in sodium; it reflects two different processed products.

Do olives provide fiber?

Yes, but portion size limits the absolute amount. At 3.3 g/100 g, a 30 g serving provides about 1 g. That contributes to the day but is not comparable with a larger serving of beans, vegetables or fruit.

How to interpret them

Olives fit well as a flavorful fat-rich food in modest portions. If sodium matters to you, the label on the actual jar is more informative than olive color. Draining brine removes liquid but does not guarantee removal of sodium already inside the fruit.

faq.question: How many calories are in olives?
faq.answer: It depends on the product. The green reference used here has 145 calories/100 g, about 44 calories in 30 g.

faq.question: What type of fat is in olives?
faq.answer: Mostly monounsaturated fat, with oleic acid as a major fatty acid.

faq.question: Are olives high in sodium?
faq.answer: They can be. The green reference contains 1,556 mg/100 g, but curing and brine create substantial product-to-product variation.

faq.question: Do olives contain fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. The green reference provides 3.3 g/100 g, about 1 g in 30 g.
